questions.q: In this lesson's comparison, what is the main latency problem with Design A (making every Meridian field a real-time callout)?
options: Every quote line waits on a network round trip even for fields that rarely change and were almost certainly already correct, adding cost with no real benefit
Design A has no latency problem at all
Design A is only slow for inventory and credit hold, the two fields that actually need to be live
Latency only matters for batch jobs, never for real-time callouts
questions.explain: Design A pays a live-callout latency cost on every field, including catalog and price, which rarely change -- meaning the user waits for an answer that a cached value would have given just as correctly.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe the difference in blast radius between Design A and Design B if the ERP has an outage?
options: Both designs fail identically during an ERP outage
Design B fails completely during any ERP outage, while Design A is fully resilient

Design A makes the entire quoting screen dependent on the ERP being reachable, so an ERP outage takes down quoting entirely; Design B's batch-synced fields keep working from cache, exposing only the two genuinely volatile fields
Neither design is affected by an ERP outage in any way
questions.explain: Because Design A makes every field a live callout, an ERP outage blocks the entire quote screen. Design B limits that exposure to only the fields that actually need real-time accuracy, keeping the rest working from cache.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against simply "picking the simpler design" when comparing Design A and Design B?
options: Because Design B is actually simpler by every possible measure

Because simplicity measured by number of patterns isn't the same as simplicity measured by the actual risk the organization carries -- Design B's added complexity is deliberately buying a reduction in blast radius and load
Because review boards never care about simplicity at all
Because Design A cannot technically be implemented in Salesforce
questions.explain: Design A looks simpler by having one pattern instead of two, but that framing ignores risk: Design B's extra complexity is specifically what reduces blast radius and system load, which a reviewer asking "simpler by which measure?" would surface.

questions.q: What does this lesson say makes a design comparison read as biased rather than reasoned to an experienced reviewer?
options: Including too many criteria in the comparison table
Admitting that the rejected design has any advantages at all
Using the word "criteria" instead of "factors"
Only listing reasons for the design you already picked, with no honest accounting of the alternative's real strengths
questions.explain: A one-sided comparison that hides the alternative's genuine strengths (like Design A's simpler build and maintenance) reads as biased. The strongest comparison names those strengths honestly and still explains why other criteria outweigh them for this case.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why can't a single uniform integration pattern optimize correctness for both Meridian's inventory field and its catalog/price fields at once?
options: Because the two groups of fields have different volatility -- real-time pays off for fast-changing data but delivers no real correctness benefit for data that rarely changes
Because correctness has nothing to do with how a field is synced
Because Salesforce only allows one integration pattern per object
Because catalog and price data cannot be cached under any circumstances
questions.explain: Correctness benefit from a real-time pattern scales with how often the underlying data actually changes. Applying the same pattern uniformly either wastes effort on slow-changing fields or under-serves fast-changing ones -- it can't be tuned for both at once.
